claims.statement: Full-text and alphabetical page audits confirm zero entries or occurrences of jamboree (and variants jambaree / jambone) in George W. Matsell's New York thieves' glossary Vocabulum; or, The Rogue's Lexicon (May 23, 1859), John Russell Bartlett's Dictionary of Americanisms across its 1st (1848) and 2nd (1859) editions (prior to its 1877 4th edition addition), and John Camden Hotten's British Slang Dictionary across all 1859–1874 editions.
claims.rationale: Direct alphabetical inspection of J-entries and full-text OCR sweeps across canonical mid-19th-century underworld cant and British metropolitan slang lexicons demonstrate that jamboree was neither inherited British flash cant nor an established pre-1859 literary Americanism when it surfaced in 1850s Bowery minstrelsy and Brooklyn saloon speech.

evidence_boundary.establishes: Complete lexicographical absence of jamboree from Matsell (1859), Bartlett (1848, 1859), and Hotten (1859–1874), contrasting with its subsequent American entry in Schele De Vere (1872) and Bartlett (1877).
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: Absence of oral vernacular circulation among New York boatmen, minstrels, or volunteer firemen prior to 1859, since slang dictionaries lag spoken innovation.
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: Whether transient 1850s New York penny-press flash glossaries outside Matsell recorded the noun before June 1858.

limitations: Published slang and Americanism dictionaries exhibit compilation lag and register selectivity; absence constrains thieves'-cant and British-import hypotheses without proving exact oral date of coinage.

claims.target_lexeme: jamboree (Trap A serial misdates and Trap D modern wrapper/paraphrase intrusions)
claims.case_section: 5. Evaluating Origin Pathways, Folk-Myth Refutations, and Trap A–D Exclusions
claims.short_label: Disqualification of 1835–1864 serial founding-year misdates and post-1930 archive wrapper hits
claims.statement: Masthead, colophon, and archival-series verification disqualifies apparent pre-1858 and Civil War hits generated by Trap A serial founding-year metadata ('1857' Atlantic Monthly = Dec. 1903; '1841' Punch = May 18, 1895; '1835' Lowell Daily Courier = Oct. 26, 1881; '1864' The Telegrapher = Dec. 11, 1875) and Trap D modern wrapper or retrospective paraphrase intrusions ('1838' Foreign Office FO 407/237 = 1958 Sudan Scout dispatch; 1878 Upham retrospective Gold Rush chapter heading vs. 1849 diary 'jollification').
claims.rationale: Checking physical volume title pages, issue mastheads, and Foreign Office series bounds eliminates every catalog-induced chronological mirage between 1835 and 1857 that would otherwise distort the 1855–1858 emergence baseline.

evidence_boundary.establishes: True publication dates (1875, 1878, 1881, 1895, 1903, and 1958) for six catalog-misdated or retrospectively framed search hits appearing under 1835–1864 metadata.
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: Absence of genuine mid-19th-century occurrences in properly dated newspapers.
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: None on the audited serial volumes; each masthead or series date is directly verified.

limitations: CERT-2500-962 (FO 407/237, 1958) is verified via National Archives (Kew) catalog series bounds (verification_level: discovered, no hosted scan due to post-1930 copyright cutoff).

evidence.reason: Proves Google Books '1857' Atlantic Monthly hit prints in Vol. XCII (December 1903, p. 817).
Proves '1841' Punch hit prints in Vol. CVIII (May 18, 1895, p. 237).
Proves '1835' Lowell Daily Courier hit prints in the October 26, 1881 issue (p. 1, col. 6).
Proves '1864' Telegrapher hit prints in Vol. XI, No. 495 (December 11, 1875, p. 297).
Proves Google Books '1838' British Foreign Office snippet ('World Scout Jamboree') belongs to FO 407/237 (Sudan Confidential Print, 1958).
Demonstrates that Upham's 1878 chapter synopsis 'Grand Jamboree' is retrospective 1878 framing over an August 6, 1849 diary entry reading 'grand jollification'.

claims.target_lexeme: jamboree (Trap B dirty-OCR ghosts and Trap C proper-noun homographs)
claims.case_section: 5. Evaluating Origin Pathways, Folk-Myth Refutations, and Trap A–D Exclusions
claims.short_label: Disqualification of 1809–1868 dirty-OCR hallucinations and Senegambian/maritime homographs
claims.statement: Zoomed letterpress and onomastic inspection disqualifies all pre-1858 OCR ghosts across Internet Archive, Google Books, BSB, and Open-ONI—1809 Nicholson ('will not be' -> 'jamboree'), 1821 Fraktur ('Samborer' -> 'Gamboree'), July 30, 1849 Pittsburgh Daily Gazette ('discharges' -> 'Jamborees'), September 12, 1853 Daily Pittsburgh Gazette ('Spear & Jackson's' -> 'Jamboree'), and April 25, 1868 Army and Navy Journal (dotted leaders)—alongside proper-noun homographs in Mungo Park's 1815 'Kingdom of Jamberoo' (Senegambia) and the 1894 Mercantile Navy List Nova Scotia yawl 'Jamboree' (misdated '1850').
claims.rationale: Direct ink inspection confirms that 100% of machine-indexed tokens of jamboree/jamborees prior to 1850–1855 are OCR character-segmentation hallucinations or unrelated proper names.

evidence_boundary.establishes: Complete paleographic and onomastic falsification of seven pre-1858/1868 OCR ghosts and proper-noun homographs across book and newspaper databases.
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: Absence of unindexed handbills or un-digitized newspapers outside the audited repositories.
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: None on the seven inspected scans; actual printed letterforms are directly legible.

limitations: Bounds OCR false-positive elimination to the indexed digital repositories audited (Open-ONI, Chronicling America, Google Books, Internet Archive, BSB).

evidence.reason: Proves 1809 British Encyclopedia OCR hit 'jamboree' actually prints 'will not be' across a degraded column gutter.
Proves 1821 German Fraktur OCR hit 'Gamboree' actually prints Galician ethnonym 'Samborer' (from Sambor).
Proves July 30, 1849 Pittsburgh Daily Gazette OCR hit 'Jamborees' actually prints medical plural 'discharges' in an Ayers' Cherry Pectoral ad.
Proves September 12, 1853 Daily Pittsburgh Gazette OCR hit 'Jamboree' actually prints Sheffield cutler 'Spear & Jackson's'.
Proves April 25, 1868 U.S. Army and Navy Journal OCR hit 'jamboree' is tabular dotted-leader noise.
Proves Mungo Park's 1815 'Kingdom of Jamberoo' is an unrelated Senegambian polity name rather than English slang.
Proves Google Books '1850' Mercantile Navy List entry for yawl 'Jamboree' (built Lunenburg, NS, 1893) actually prints in the May 1894 volume.
